**al-Ḥubuk** (the paths, the lines of patterning): like the patterns of sand and water when the wind strikes them. Likewise the *ḥubk* of hair: the traces that fold and break it. Zuhayr said:

Crowned with the roots of the stars, woven by a cold wind over its bright surface, its patterns
until it sought help from water with no rope to draw it, among the wide valleys, with pools at its edges.

Crowned with the roots of the stars, woven by a cold wind over its bright surface, its patterns.

As the sand-grouse sought help from a bright, pale, flowing... fearing the eyes, and the *ḥashk* did not wait for her.

[[The poem describes a sand-grouse (*qaṭāh*) that fled from a *ṣafr* (a dry, empty place) until it sought water nearby with no rope to draw it. *Lā rishā' lahu* means there is no rope by which to draw from it, because it is not needed, since it lies among the wide, level valleys (*al-abāṭiḥ*), that is, in spacious, flat places. If he means the place of the water, then *min* is explanatory (*bayāniyya*). *Fī ḥawāshihi* means on its sides. *Al-birak* is the plural of *birka* (pool), like *ruṭab* and *ruṭba*, and the sand-grouse is a kind of water bird. "Crowned with the roots of the stars" means the water is covered with plants that have no stalks. Another version reads "with long stars," meaning tall ones. "Tansijuhu" means it folds it in a regular manner, like weaving, so this is an explicit metaphor.

*Al-kharīq* (with a qāf) is the cold and the swift in its course. *Al-ḍāḥī* is the manifest. *Al-ḥubk* is the path on the face of water when the wind strikes it, plural of *ḥabbāk* or *ḥabīka*. *Al-sayy'* (with a fatḥa or kasra) is the milk at the tip of the teat. *Al-fazz* is the young of a wild cow.

*Al-ghaytala* is dense, intertwined trees, so the attribution of *fazz* to it is because the fawn is in it. It is also said that it is the wild cow. *Al-ʿuyūn* here means the hunters' watchmen and spies. *Ḥashaka al-darra bi-l-laban* means the udder became full of milk. The vowel of *al-ḥashk* here is moved for metrical necessity, meaning she did not wait for the udder to fill. By my life, this plea was a fine one. This indicates that she was thirsty.]]

The garment is *maḥbuka* because its rings are beaten into lines. It is said that the creation of the heaven is also like this. From al-Ḥasan: *ḥubkuhā* means its stars. The meaning is that they adorn it as the embroidered garment is adorned with the lines of embroidery. It is also said that *ḥubkuhā* means its firmness and solidity, from the saying "a horse with *maḥbūk al-maʿāqim*" [[His saying "a horse with *maḥbūk al-maʿāqim*": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, *al-maʿāqim* of horses are the joints. The pastern near the hoof is a *maʿqam*, the knee is a *maʿqam*, and the hock is a *maʿqam*. (ʿ)]], meaning its joints are firm. When the weaver weaves well, they say: "How fine his *ḥubk* is!" It is the plural of *ḥabāk*, like *mithāl* and *mithl*, or of *ḥabīka*, like *ṭarīqa* and *ṭuruq*.

It has been read as *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-qufl*, *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-silk*, *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-jabal*, *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-barq*, *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-niʿam*, and *al-ḥubk* on the pattern of *al-ibil*.

﴿إِنَّكُمْ لَفِي قَوْلٍ مُخْتَلِفٍ﴾ "Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying." This is their saying about the Messenger: a sorcerer, a poet, and a madman; and about the Qur'an: poetry, sorcery, and the fables of the ancients. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the saying of the disbelievers is not consistent; rather it is contradictory and varied. From Qatādah: among you is one who confirms and one who denies, and one who acknowledges and one who rejects.

﴿يُؤْفَكُ عَنْهُ﴾ "he is turned away from it." The pronoun refers to the Qur'an or to the Messenger, meaning he is turned away from it, from *ṣarf* (turning), the turning which has no greater turning than it. [[Maḥmūd said: "*yuṣrafu ʿanhu* from *ṣarf*, the turning that has no greater turning..." Aḥmad said: This arrangement only conveys the meaning mentioned earlier. If you say "*yuṣrafu ʿanhu min ṣarf*," the hearer knows that your saying "*yuṣrafu ʿanhu*" suffices without "*min ṣarf*," because by itself it is like a repetition of the first. Were it not for the benefit that is sensed in it, which prevents making it a repetition, that benefit is this: when you single this out as the one who was turned away, you convey that others were not turned away. It is as if you said: turning truly belongs only to this one, and every other turning is, relative to it, no turning. And God knows best.]] and greater, like his saying: "None perishes before God except the one who is destined to perish." Its origin is the invocation of killing and destruction, and then it came to be used in the sense of "curse" and "condemnation." Al-kharrasun are the liars who conjecture what is not sound, and they are the people of the divergent speech. The definite article (al-) indicates them, as if it were said: "Destroyed are these conjecturers." It is also read qutila al-kharrasin (with the genitive), meaning: "May God destroy the conjecturers."

Fi ghamratin (in a flood of heedlessness): in ignorance that engulfs them. Sahun (heedless): unmindful of what they were commanded. Yas'aluna (they ask), fa-yaqulun ayyana yawmu al-din (﴿When is the Day of Judgment?﴾), i.e., when is the Day of Recompense? It is also read with a kasra on the hamza (ayyana with i), and this is a dialect form.

If you say: How is ayyan (when) used as an adverb of yawm (day), when ahyan (times) are only used as adverbs of events (hadathan)? I say: its meaning is: "When is the occurrence of the Day of Judgment?"

It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative because it is attached to a non-declinable element, namely a clause. If you say: What is its position when it is in the accusative? I say: its position may be accusative by the hidden verb "will occur," and nominative as "it is the day when they will be tried upon the Fire." It is also permissible for hadha to be a substitute (badal) for fitnatakum, i.e., "taste this punishment."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 51, verses 20–21:**

There are signs in the earth ﴿for those with certainty﴾ that point to the Maker, His power, His wisdom and His governance, in that it is spread out as a carpet for what is upon it, as He says: ﴿He Who made the earth a cradle for you﴾ (43:10). In it are roads and wide passages for those who move about in it and walk through its shoulders (i.e., its far reaches). It is divided into parts: plains and mountains, land and sea, and adjoining tracts that are hard and soft, and ʿadhāh [[His words "ʿadhāh" in al-Sihah: "al-ʿadhāh" is good soil, plural ʿadhawāt. (ʿ)]] and saline. It is like a mare (ṭarūqa) that is impregnated with various plants and kinds of trees, with fruits of differing colours, tastes and fragrances, watered with one water, ﴿and We favour some of them over others in fruit﴾ (13:4). All of it is suited to the needs, benefits and interests of its inhabitants, in their health and their sickness. There are also in it the gushing springs, the minerals that are dazzling, and the creatures that are scattered over its land and sea, differing in form, shape and action: wild and domestic animals, insects, and other things. ﴿For those with certainty﴾ means the monotheists who have taken the sound, demonstrative path that leads to knowledge. They are observers with seeing eyes and penetrating understandings; whenever they see a sign, they know the manner of its contemplation, so their faith increases upon their faith and their certainty upon their certainty.

﴿And in yourselves﴾ (51:21): in their beginning and in their transitions from one state to another, and in their inner and outer parts there are wonders of natural disposition and marvels of creation at which minds are bewildered. Consider the hearts and what is placed in them of intellects, and what they are given of kinds of meanings; and the tongues, speech, and the points of articulation of letters, and what is in their composition, arrangement and subtleties: these are shining signs and decisive proofs of the wisdom of the Governor. Leave aside the hearing, the sight, the limbs and the rest of the bodily members, and their suitability for what they were created for, and the joints placed in the limbs for bending and flexing. For when one of these stiffens (jasā), weakness comes; and when one becomes slack, humiliation settles in. ﴿So blessed is God, the Best of Creators﴾ (23:14).

And in the sky is your provision, and that which you are promised. (Qur'an 51:22)

It is the rain, because it is the cause of sustenance. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it is the snow and every constantly flowing spring derived from it. It is related from al-Hasan that when he saw clouds he would say to his companions: "By God, your provision is in it, but you are deprived of it because of your sins." And that which you are promised, namely Paradise: it is upon the back of the seventh heaven, beneath the Throne.

Or it may mean that all that you are provided with in this world and all that you are promised in the Hereafter is decreed and written in the sky.

It has been read as: مثل (mithla) with a raised vowel as an attribute of al-Haqq, meaning "truth like your speech," and with a fatha as: "indeed it is truth, truly, like your speech."

It is also permissible that it be fatha because it is annexed to something indeclinable (ghayr mutamakkin). Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 51, verse 31–37:

When he (Abraham) knew that they were angels, and that they do not descend except as messengers by the permission of God in certain matters, he said: ﴿What is your business, then?﴾ That is: what is your affair, and what is your errand, ﴿O messengers?﴾ ﴿...to a people of criminals,﴾ meaning the people of Lot, ﴿to send upon them stones of clay,﴾ meaning: sijjil (baked clay), which is clay baked the way bricks are baked, until it becomes as hard as stones, ﴿marked﴾ (musawwamah), meaning marked, from al-sawmah, which is a sign on each one of them bearing the name of the one who is to be destroyed by it. It is also said: it was made known that these were stones of punishment.

It is also said: with a sign indicating that they were not stones of this world. He called them ﴿transgressors﴾ (musrifin), just as he called them ﴿aggressors﴾ (adin), because of their extravagance and their transgression in their deeds, in that they were not content with what had been made lawful for them. The pronoun in ﴿therein﴾ refers to the town (al-qaryah), though no mention of it has preceded, because it is well known. In it is evidence that faith (iman) and submission (islam) are one, and that they are both attributes of praise. ﴿Therein﴾: it is said they were Lot and his two daughters. It is also said that Lot and the members of his household who were saved numbered thirteen. Qatadah reported: "Had there been more than that in it, He would have saved them, so that they would know that faith is protected, and that none of its people are lost in the sight of God."

﴿A sign﴾: a sign by which those who fear are admonished, but not those whose hearts are hardened. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the layered stone (sakhr mandud) in it. It is also said: it is black, foul water.

Until an appointed time. Its exegesis is His saying: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days." So they defied the command of their Lord and were arrogant in not complying with it. It was recited as al-ṣaʿqa (the single blast), which denotes one occurrence, from the verbal noun of "the thunderbolt struck them." The thunderbolt itself is the descending bolt. "While they were looking on" means it was in daytime and they were witnessing it. It is related that the Amalekites were with them in the valley, watching them, and it did not harm them. "So they were not able to stand up" is like His saying: "So they awoke in their homes, lying prostrate." It was also said that this is from their saying "I cannot stand up to it" (mā yaqūmu bihi), when one is unable to repel it. "Defending themselves" means those who could ward off the punishment.

"And of every thing We have created pairs, that you may take heed." (The verse, 51:49, is rendered as: And of all things We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember.)

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary:

"And of every thing": i.e., from among all living creatures, "We created pairs," a male and a female. It is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that he said: the heavens and the earth, the night and the day, the sun and the moon, the land and the sea, death and life. He enumerated things and said: every two of them are a pair, while Allah the Exalted is singular, having no like.

"That you may remember": i.e., We did all of that, the construction of the heaven, the spreading of the earth, and the creation of the pairs, intending that you might remember, so that you would know the Creator and worship Him.

So turn away from them, and turn away from those to whom you repeatedly conveyed the call but who did not respond, and whose obstinacy and contentiousness you have come to know. Meaning: "I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me, and I did not intend from all of them anything but that." The apparent context of the verse is evidence for the people of the Sunnah, for it was brought only to declare the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that His dealings with His servants cannot be compared to the dealings of created masters with their slaves. For the slaves of creatures are required to serve and earn for their masters, and through the earnings of their slaves masters obtain their provision. Allah, exalted is He, does not require from His servants provision or food, but requires from them only their worship and nothing else. Beyond the fact that He does not require provision from them, He is the One who provides for them. This noble meaning is what is adorned under the banner of this verse, for it was brought for it and speaks by it. But desire blinds and deafens. And success is from Allah.]]. If you say: if He intended worship from all of them, would they all be worshippers? I say: He intended that they worship Him by choice, not by compulsion, since He created them with capacity (to choose), so some of them chose to abandon worship while He intended it. Had He intended it by force and constraint, it would have been found in all of them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 51, verse 57–58:

He means: My relationship with My servants is not like the relationship of masters with their slaves. The owners of slaves own them so that they may be helped in obtaining their livelihoods and sustenance: either one who equips them for trade in order to gain profit, or one who employs them in farming in order to cultivate land, or one who hires them out in a craft so that he benefits from their wages, or one who sends them to gather firewood, or to gather grass, or to cook, or to bake, and whatever is similar to these works and occupations that are devoted to the means of subsistence and the avenues of provision. As for the Owner of the slaves, He says to them: "Busy yourselves with what benefits you in yourselves; I do not wish to employ you in obtaining My provision or your provision. I am Self-sufficient, needing neither you nor your services, and I bestow upon you your provision and whatever sustains and maintains you from Myself."
